text: Patterns such as infinite scroll, autoplaying videos, or requiring an account just to make a purchase all interfere with the users control over their own experience. <break time="0.8s" /> From a sustainability perspective, many of these patterns encourage overconsumption of data and attention. <break time="0.8s" /> Infinite scroll keeps loading new content whether the user wants it or not, increasing data usage and device processing. <break time="0.8s" /> Autoplay forces media to load and play even for people who may never watch it. <break time="0.8s" /> These choices consume more energy on both the users device and the servers delivering the content. <break time="0.8s" /> Take the decision by a popular music streaming platform to replace static album artwork with short video loops by default. <break time="0.8s" /> This change significantly increases data usage and battery consumption, while the option to disable it is buried deep in the settings. <break time="0.8s" /> As a result, most users consume more resources unless they actively search for a way to opt out. <break time="0.8s" /> It is important to acknowledge that web design always nudges behavior in some way. <break time="0.8s" /> Showing consequences and highlighting options are all forms of influence. <break time="0.8s" /> The ethical line is not whether nudging exists, but whether it is transparent, reversible, and aligned with the users interests. <break time="0.8s" /> In many cases, the most responsible approach is to make the lower impact option the default, while keeping alternatives clearly available. <break time="0.8s" /> Defaults are powerful, and when chosen carefully, they can reduce environmental impact without removing user agency.
